title: A pressure plan with a prospectively tested earthquake bound

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a way to forecast the earthquake consequences of a specified reservoir pressure plan before carrying it out. Before materially changing depletion or injection, an operator would publish the pressure and operating schedule, an upper bound on earthquake magnitude, and a forecast of the number of events above a chosen magnitude over a defined period. Observations during and after implementation would then test those predictions. This is a proposed capability, not an achievement established by the supplied evidence.

Conceptual synthesis: the advance would connect reservoir behavior, fault mechanics and uncertainty estimation closely enough to make a prospective forecast useful for an operating decision. It would need to distinguish a claimed physical ceiling on earthquake size from a probabilistic upper bound with a stated chance of exceedance. A retrospective fit can help build the model, but only predictions recorded before the relevant operating change can demonstrate prospective performance. Forecasting consequences would support pressure planning; it would not itself establish control over earthquake rupture.

significance.text: Groningen illustrates the operational stakes. In its announcement of 23 June 2023, the Dutch government linked the planned end of gas production to induced earthquakes and their consequences after sixty years of production. The state secretary also warned that earthquakes would continue for years. This provides a concrete motivation for assessing seismic consequences before changing operations, including consequences that may persist after production stops.

Conditional significance: useful, calibrated forecasts could make seismic hazard an explicit constraint when choosing depletion and injection schedules. Operators could compare proposed pressure plans against declared earthquake-risk limits before committing to them. The revolutionary step would be demonstrating reliable, decision-relevant prediction under an actual operating change, rather than merely explaining the earthquakes after they occur.

Limits and downstream possibilities: even a successful forecast would not guarantee that a safe, economically useful production rate exists. An acceptable plan might still require curtailment or shutdown, and keeping events below a magnitude bound would not by itself establish acceptable damage or risk. Produced-water disposal is a plausible application of the same forecasting capability, but transfer from depletion to injection would require separate validation. Water treatment, building codes and compensation address different parts of the problem and remain outside this technical test.

missing_breakthrough.text: Proposed scientific target: predict how a declared pressure history changes the likelihood, size and timing of fault slip, with uncertainty narrow enough to guide an operating decision. The research identifies pressure diffusion, poroelastic stress changes and friction as mechanisms that the framework would need to connect. Their contribution to a successful prospective forecast is not established by an inspectable scientific source in this evidence set; they remain the proposed mechanistic basis of the innovation.

Engineering synthesis: the model would need to represent pressure propagation and stress changes beyond the directly observed reservoir, identify which faults could slip, and account for uncertain fault geometry, initial stress and frictional properties. Predicting the largest earthquake also requires addressing how far a rupture could propagate after it starts. Unmapped faults and poorly constrained subsurface conditions could therefore limit the usefulness of a bound even when the modeled reservoir pressure is accurate. The supplied material does not resolve whether these uncertainties can be reduced sufficiently, or whether a useful capability is attainable in every intended setting.

Statistical synthesis: an expected earthquake count is not a ceiling on the observed count, and observing no event above a magnitude bound does not establish that exceedance was impossible. The breakthrough therefore includes uncertainty quantification and prospective evaluation, alongside physical modeling. Bounds must be informative enough to distinguish operating choices, and repeated forecasts must be assessed for calibration. A very broad bound or one quiet trial could satisfy a superficial test without demonstrating useful predictive skill.

current_state.text: The retained government announcement, dated 23 June 2023, stated that Groningen gas production would stop on 1 October 2023 after sixty years. It nevertheless retained exceptional provisions for limited restart during the following gas year and described definitive closure of the remaining eleven production locations from 1 October 2024 as a future step. The announcement also identified the annual production decision as a draft. It documents the announced policy and its qualifications, rather than verifying subsequent implementation.

The same announcement warned that earthquakes would continue for years after production stopped. That warning supports including delayed consequences in the proposed forecasting problem. It does not quantify how curtailment changes seismicity, prove that shutdown immediately removes hazard, or document later dismantling. The supplied review reports complete retained text for this announcement, with no extraction issues; its limitation here is the scope and date of the announcement.

The supplied research identifies a 2024 paper by Julian J. Bommer, Jan van Elk and Mark D. Zoback on Groningen maximum-magnitude estimation. It attributes to that paper proponent estimates around magnitude 4–5, an upper tail reaching magnitude 7 in a 2016 panel distribution, and subsequent narrowing of an expert logic tree. Although the earlier research says an accepted manuscript was inspected, the supplied source index contains no retained artifact or extracted text for the DOI. The validated review therefore could not verify the paper's identity and contents, those numerical details, or the interpretation of the logic-tree history. These figures remain unverified attributions in this record; the missing artifact is not evidence that they are false.

Evidence boundary: the supplied material establishes a dated operational motivation, but does not establish a demonstrated pressure plan with the proposed prospective earthquake bound. It also does not establish that such a capability is globally unavailable. The bounded search record supplied to the review was empty, and no inspectable scientific artifact or later implementation evidence resolves the state of forecasting or Groningen closure as of November 2026. Retrospective estimation and prospective validation must remain distinct, but the available material cannot support an exhaustive judgment about either field's current achievements.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration, not an established standard: before a material depletion or injection change, publish the pressure plan, operating schedule, evaluation period, monitored region, magnitude definition and event-count threshold. State the maximum-magnitude bound, whether it is a physical ceiling or a probabilistic bound, the forecast count above the threshold, and uncertainty intervals or predictive distributions. Define success and failure before implementation, including what departures from the declared operating plan would mean for the test.
completion_criteria.label: Preregister pressure plan, earthquake forecasts, and trial success criteria

completion_criteria.text: Proposed evaluation: implement the declared plan, document actual operating conditions, and compare the resulting earthquake observations with the registered forecasts. Require bounds narrow enough to change or justify an operating decision, and evaluate count forecasts as uncertain predictions rather than requiring observed counts to equal their expected values. Include an observation period appropriate to possible delayed seismicity. Retrospective fitting alone would not meet this proposal, and a traffic-light response that changes operations after shaking begins would not substitute for the prospective test. Any such intervention would need to be recorded and incorporated into interpretation of the trial.
completion_criteria.label: Prospectively test decision-relevant earthquake bounds and uncertain count forecasts

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries: repeat the demonstration in a second geological setting, with accessible operating records, monitoring data, model assumptions and evaluation methods sufficient for independent assessment. Evaluate calibration across repeated forecasts; one uneventful trial cannot establish a reliable rare-event bound. Demonstrations should state the geological conditions, pressure ranges, operating rates and forecast horizons for which performance has been shown. Successful finite tests would establish demonstrated breadth within those conditions, not literal universality or a guarantee against all larger earthquakes.
completion_criteria.label: Reproduce across geological settings, reporting forecast calibration and performance limits

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: PET-01, “Blind prediction of multiphase reservoir flow,” shares the demand for predictions tested against outcomes withheld from model development. Flow prediction could inform pressure histories, but successful prediction of fluid movement would not by itself establish earthquake magnitude or event-count bounds. PET-08, “Permeability and saturation measured through the reservoir volume,” could improve knowledge of fluid pathways and pressure propagation; those measurements would still leave fault geometry, stress and friction to be constrained.

Roster-based synthesis: PET-02, “Conventional-oil recovery at gas-field recovery factors,” and PET-05, “Shale-oil recovery from the matrix,” concern accessing a greater share of hydrocarbons. PET-10 concerns the seismic consequences of the pressure plans used to pursue production. Better recovery and a prospectively tested earthquake forecast are separate achievements: neither guarantees the other, and a validated forecast might identify a seismic constraint on a recovery strategy.

Roster-based synthesis: PET-03, “Commercial gas production from methane hydrate,” and PET-04, “Industrial in-situ conversion of oil-shale kerogen,” concern different resource-production capabilities. Where their operating plans change subsurface pressure or stress, they could create settings in which PET-10's forecasting approach is relevant. That possible overlap does not establish common governing behavior or justify transferring a bound without validation in the relevant geology and process.

Roster-based synthesis: PET-06, “Hydrogen from petroleum reservoirs, with the other products left underground,” and PET-11, “In-reservoir conversion of bitumen to pipeline-specification crude,” concern subsurface conversion and product handling. Their pressure-management requirements could intersect with seismic forecasting, but successful conversion or retention of products underground would not demonstrate PET-10. Conversely, an earthquake forecast would not establish conversion efficiency, product quality or containment.

Roster-based synthesis: PET-07, “Deep well construction without a steep depth penalty,” concerns the cost and feasibility of accessing depth; it could enable operations or monitoring without solving fault-response prediction. PET-09, “Bitumen that flows at native reservoir temperature,” concerns fluid mobility. Any resulting pressure plan would still need its own seismic assessment. These remain distinct innovations even where they are used in the same development.

unresolved_issues: The cited scientific paper's identity, numerical estimates, expert logic-tree history and relevance to prospective validation remain unverified within the supplied evidence.
The supplied material does not verify Groningen's subsequent closure, restart history or dismantling after the June 2023 announcement.
Whether a useful pressure-plan forecasting capability has been demonstrated elsewhere, or since the supplied sources, remains unassessed.
The intended magnitude bound still needs a precise interpretation: a claimed physical ceiling or a probabilistic bound with a specified exceedance probability.
Acceptable uncertainty, decision-relevant bound width, monitoring completeness, evaluation duration and sufficient repeated trials remain to be defined for particular applications.
Transferability between depletion and injection, including produced-water disposal, requires evidence from the relevant operating and geological settings.
It remains uncertain whether unobserved faults and poorly constrained stress and friction permit useful bounds at economically relevant operating rates.

brief.title: Earthquake forecasts for underground pressure plans
possible: Before changing how much gas they extract or water they inject underground, operators could compare pressure plans by their predicted earthquakes. Each forecast would state an upper limit on earthquake size and how many earthquakes to expect above a chosen size.
People could then test those forecasts against what actually happens, including earthquakes that occur after operations stop.
why: Earthquake risk could become an explicit constraint on operating plans. Operators could use forecasts to decide whether to proceed, reduce operations or shut down before committing to a pressure change.

sources.showed: The government announced plans to stop Groningen gas production because of its consequences for residents. It warned that earthquakes would continue for years.
sources.cited_for: Groningen illustrates why pressure planning needs to account for earthquakes that persist after production stops.
sources.not_established: The announcement does not measure how a pressure change affects earthquakes or demonstrate a successful forecast.

sources.who: Julian J. Bommer, Jan van Elk and Mark D. Zoback
sources.showed: This paper examines estimates of the largest earthquake that gas production could cause in Groningen.
sources.cited_for: The work addresses estimating the largest earthquake associated with gas production.
sources.not_established: Estimating earthquake size does not establish that forecasts made before an operating change reliably predict its consequences.

shown: A pressure plan with a successfully tested advance forecast remains a proposed capability. Explaining past earthquakes or estimating their largest possible size does not demonstrate reliable prediction before operations change.
missing: A model linking underground pressure changes to fault movement, with uncertainty small enough to guide operating choices.
A successful advance test of earthquake size limits and event counts, including delayed earthquakes.
Repeated successful forecasts across geological settings, with clear limits on where they work.

milestones.label: The pressure plan and forecasts are declared before operations change
milestones.explanation: Operators would publish the pressure schedule, forecast size limit, uncertain event counts, monitoring scope and success criteria before changing operations. This would make the predictions testable.

milestones.label: Advance forecasts guide decisions and withstand an operating trial
milestones.explanation: A trial would compare recorded operations and earthquakes with the advance forecasts, allowing for uncertain counts and delayed shaking. Useful size limits would have to help justify or change an operating decision.

milestones.label: Repeated forecasts work across geological settings with stated limits
milestones.explanation: Trials in a second geological setting would allow independent assessment and test whether repeated outcomes match forecast probabilities. Stated operating and geological limits would define where the forecasts have worked.

uncertain: Does the size limit mean a physically impossible larger earthquake, or a larger earthquake with a stated chance of occurring?
Can unknown faults and uncertain underground stresses allow useful forecasts at economically useful operating rates?
How narrow must forecasts be, and how long and often must they be tested, to establish reliable performance?

page.title: Prospective forecasting of induced seismicity
page.definition: Forecasts give earthquake-count distributions and largest-event exceedance probabilities conditional on a specified extraction or injection schedule. Independent observations during operations and after shut-in, when flow stops, test their consistency and predictive skill.

goal.need: On 23 June 2023, the Dutch government announced the end of Groningen gas production after 60 years and warned that earthquakes would continue for years. The largest Groningen earthquake in the record assessed in 2024 was the 16 August 2012 Huizinge event, local magnitude 3.6. Operating decisions therefore concern both earthquake frequency and size, including seismicity after production stops.

completion.title: Pressure-plan forecasts pass independent prospective consistency and benchmark tests.
completion.criterion: Forecasts archived before an operating change, conditional on the implemented pressure and flow schedule, pass independently administered CSEP number and magnitude consistency tests at 5% significance. Their mean information gain, the log-likelihood improvement per earthquake over a predeclared benchmark, has a 95% confidence interval wholly above zero. Forecasts include count and largest-event exceedance distributions for a specified region, magnitude threshold and period, including a declared post-operation interval. The magnitude bound is a probability quantile. Duration and sample size are application-specific.
completion.set_by: Atlas synthesis of published earthquake-forecast tests; no outside body located specifies this combined pressure-plan completion test.
completion.basis: DOE/NETL, SED and IEAGHG guidance, CSEP protocols and the 2024 forecasting expert review yielded no joint pressure-plan completion standard. The review found that “specific tests it should pass could not be identified.” This composite combines published consistency and comparative tests. Passage demonstrates site-specific forecast skill; it does not establish a physical magnitude ceiling or calibration of rare extremes.

milestones.title: Controlled pressure changes reproduce a fault-reactivation threshold predicted from rock tests.
milestones.criterion: Measure reservoir-rock friction and in situ stress, predict a fault-reactivation condition, and reproduce the predicted activation and suppression of seismicity during controlled pressure changes. At Rangely, one oil field, the predicted critical pressure was 257 bar (25.7 MPa); a complete pressure cycle across it was obtained between December 1972 and May 1973. This numerical pressure is site-specific.
milestones.set_by: US Geological Survey investigators, Rangely experimental protocol reported by Raleigh, Healy and Bredehoeft in 1976; published for water injection and withdrawal.
milestones.threshold_quote: 257 bars as the critical fluid pressure above which earthquakes should be triggered.

milestones.title: A reservoir-operation forecast passes a 95% earthquake-count test on withheld observations.
milestones.criterion: The withheld count above a declared magnitude falls within the forecast's 95% predictive interval. Monitoring must reliably detect events above that cutoff. A 2025 replay found the Bayesian rate model EM1-BMAP passing throughout injection at Grimsel (9 February 2017; 1,157 catalogue events at or above completeness magnitude −5.29) and Bedretto (22 June 2022 to 23 June 2022; 5,669 at or above −4.10). Groningen's updated 2023 model assigned its withheld count 9%–11% exceedance probability. These evaluations used existing observations.
milestones.set_by: Induced Seismicity Test Bench, Király-Proag and colleagues, 2016, section 3.3; the protocol was developed for geothermal injection.
milestones.threshold_quote: the number of observed earthquakes falls within the 95% confidence interval of the forecast.

milestones.title: An issued reservoir-operation forecast passes a 5% prospective earthquake-count test.
milestones.criterion: An unchanged forecast is evaluated on earthquakes recorded after publication under its declared operating schedule. At 5% significance, the CSEP number test requires both P(N≥Nobs)>0.025 and P(N≤Nobs)>0.025. The 2023 evaluation of the 2017 Groningen forecast found extraction about 35% below its lowest scenario. After retrospective volume scaling, 10 M≥2.5 events from 1 February 2017 to 1 July 2022 lay at about 2% exceedance. The authors identified underprediction and uncertainty about the scaling correction.
milestones.set_by: CSEP number-test convention, documented in pyCSEP, Theory of CSEP Tests; prospective and pseudoprospective application is described in the 2023 Groningen evaluation.
milestones.threshold_quote: for a required significance level of 0.05, a forecast is consistent if both \(\delta_1\) and \(\delta_2\) are greater than 0.025.

not_found: No independently administered prospective study demonstrating the combined completion test was located.
No published minimum sample size or monitoring duration for validating pressure-plan magnitude-exceedance probabilities was found.
No controlled depletion experiment meeting m1 was identified.
Full texts of the 2025 subcritical-stress and 2026 model-comparison studies of Groningen could not be opened.

results.finding: At one Rangely oil field, a controlled injection and withdrawal cycle reproduced the predicted 257-bar seismicity threshold.
results.detail: Rock-friction tests and in situ stress measurements informed the prediction. Seismicity rose as pressure increased and ceased near the wells after backflow began. An earlier reinjection to 265 bars produced less than one earthquake per month.

results.finding: Groningen 2025: 7 M≥1.5 earthquakes were observed within the forecast 95% range of 0–7.
results.detail: The 2023 forecast assumed zero gas extraction from October 2023. The reported range and observed count bear on prospective consistency, but the text does not give both CSEP tail probabilities needed to establish a pass.
results.quote:
Zoals in antwoord 8 aangegeven lag de verwachting in 2025 op 5 aardbevingen,
met een bereik van 0 tot 7.

results.finding: Groningen’s 2025 forecast: 7 earthquakes of magnitude 1.5 or higher, within the 95% range of 0–7.
results.detail: The 2023 forecast preceded the 2025 observations and assumed zero production from October 2023. The text does not establish reliable detection at the stated magnitude cutoff.
results.quote:
